questions.prompt: What is the simplest way to serve your frontend and static files locally in Node.js?

options.text: Use Express static middleware (express.static('public')).
options.why: It's one line and exactly what the middleware is for.

options.text: Manually read every single image byte by byte in a custom loop.
options.why: That reinvents something that already exists, and wastes your hackathon hours.

options.text: Compile a brand new binary every time a page loads.
options.why: Way too heavy. Static files just need to be served.

questions.prompt: For a hackathon MVP, what should your pitch say about your target audience?

options.text: Targeting 50 million enterprise clients globally on day one.
options.why: Too broad. Judges don't believe you can reach everyone at once.

options.text: Solving one core pain point for a specific user group cleanly.
options.why: A specific group with a clear pain point is credible and easy to picture.

options.text: Ignoring users entirely and talking about the background graphics.
options.why: Judges want to hear who it helps, not how it looks.

questions.prompt: What happens if your external API goes down during your live presentation?

options.text: Panic and shut down the computer.
options.why: Panic loses the room. Have a plan instead.

options.text: Have local fallback data or a recorded demo ready to rescue it.
options.why: A backup plan keeps the pitch going when things fail.

options.text: Blame the hackathon Wi-Fi router.
options.why: Even if it's true, excuses don't help the judges see your project.

questions.prompt: How should you open a two minute pitch?

options.text: Start with a real person who has the problem and what goes wrong for them.
options.why: A human problem gets attention before any tech talk.

options.text: List every team member's major and the tools you used.
options.why: That can come later. Open with why anyone should care.

options.text: Say 'um, so we kind of built a thing' and start the demo.
options.why: A vague opening wastes your best seconds.

questions.prompt: A judge looks confused during your demo. What is the best response?

options.text: Talk faster so you can fit everything in.
options.why: More speed means more confusion.

options.text: Pause, simplify, and walk through the one main flow again.
options.why: Simple and slow beats complete and confusing.

options.text: Skip to the next slide and hope it gets clearer.
options.why: You'd leave the judge behind.

questions.prompt: How do you handle traffic spikes and avoid API rate limits?

options.text: Send thousands of requests synchronously on every button click.
options.why: That's how you hit rate limits instantly.

options.text: Add a timeout and fall back to cached data when the API is slow.
options.why: Caching plus a fallback keeps the demo working.

options.text: Turn the server off when traffic increases.
options.why: That means the demo is down exactly when people look.

questions.prompt: What is your long-term sustainability strategy?

options.text: A freemium plan with limits for heavy users.
options.why: It's a believable model that matches how the product is used.

options.text: Rely on free cloud credits that never expire.
options.why: Credits run out. Judges know that.

options.text: Charge users five dollars every time they view a page.
options.why: Users would leave immediately.

questions.prompt: Why should we award you the grand prize over everyone else?

options.text: Because our idea solves a real problem, works live, and we can explain why it matters.
options.why: A real problem, a working demo and a clear message is a winning combination.

options.text: Because we didn't have time to test it, but it looks really cool.
options.why: Untested and flashy rarely wins.

options.text: Because we spent all our time on custom fonts.
options.why: Polish matters less than a working idea.

questions.prompt: A judge asks: 'Who are your competitors?' What's your best answer?

options.text: We have no competitors.
options.why: Almost every idea has alternatives. Saying none sounds naive.

options.text: Two real alternatives people use today, and the specific gap we fill.
options.why: Naming real alternatives shows you did your homework.

options.text: They're all bad, ours is just better.
options.why: Dismissing others without specifics is not convincing.

questions.prompt: Your demo hits a bug on screen. What do you do?

options.text: Stop and debug live while the judges wait.
options.why: Live debugging burns your few minutes.

options.text: Acknowledge it in one sentence, switch to your backup, and keep going.
options.why: Calm recovery shows professionalism.

options.text: Blame the teammate who wrote that part.
options.why: Blaming a teammate looks worse than the bug.

questions.prompt: You have 30 seconds left. What do you say?

options.text: Rush through all your remaining slides.
options.why: Nobody can follow that.

options.text: Restate the problem, your solution, and what you'd do next.
options.why: A clean wrap-up is what judges remember.

options.text: Apologize that you ran out of time.
options.why: An apology is the last thing you want them to remember.

questions.prompt: 'What would you build next with another month?' Best answer?

options.text: Everything on our feature list.
options.why: No priorities means no plan.

options.text: One prioritized next step based on what users told us.
options.why: Specific and user-driven shows maturity.

options.text: Nothing, it's finished.
options.why: Judges want to see you can grow the idea.
